content: 1. Leprosy presents with specific clinical signs, including pale or reddish skin patches that lack sensation, numbness or tingling in the hands or feet, weakness in the hands, feet, or eyelids, painful or tender nerves, swelling or lumps on the face or earlobes, and painless wounds or burns on the hands or feet. 2. Early detection of leprosy, combined with appropriate treatment, is critical to preventing disability, simplifying treatment, and halting the transmission of the disease. 3. There is no need to fear leprosy, as it is a manageable condition similar to other diseases. Individuals affected by leprosy should not face discrimination. Once treatment begins, patients are no longer infectious within a few weeks, allowing them to work, study, marry, and live normal lives. 4. Support from family and the community is essential for individuals affected by leprosy. This support encourages adherence to multidrug therapy (MDT) and other prescribed treatments, as well as helps them reintegrate into normal life. 5. Developing culturally sensitive and standardized educational materials for patients and communities is vital to effectively communicate key messages and support healthcare workers in their efforts. 6. Newly diagnosed individuals should receive counseling and assistance to ensure timely and effective treatment. They should be educated on the following: They can lead a normal life. Where to seek answers to questions about leprosy. Where to access diagnosis and treatment. Leprosy is caused by a germ, not hereditary, and not a result of sin or a curse. Leprosy is curable, with treatment lasting 6 to 12 months. MDT may cause side effects such as red urine (in all cases) and skin darkening (in multibacillary cases). Daily medication is required, and a new blister pack is needed every 28 days. Consultations and treatment are free of charge in the public sector. Once treatment begins, leprosy is no longer infectious, but close contacts may already be at higher risk and should be examined. Skin patches may take time to disappear. Leprosy reactions can occur during or after treatment and require prompt medical attention. Signs of leprosy reactions include sudden redness and swelling of patches, pain or numbness in limbs, weakness in hands or feet, and eye problems such as pain, redness, or vision loss. Existing disabilities may or may not improve with treatment. Skills to prevent and manage disabilities may need to be learned. Locations of services for disability prevention and management, including reconstructive surgery, should be identified. 7. Awareness campaigns should target high-risk groups and communities with a high burden of leprosy. These campaigns must be tailored to the audience and supported by other sectors, such as education and social welfare, to ensure effective delivery of messages. 8. Awareness efforts should include public figures, community leaders, spiritual leaders, media, and international organizations to reduce stigma and promote understanding of leprosy. 9. Healthcare workers outside the leprosy care network should be sensitized to enhance detection and care. Training materials should be updated and aligned with national health programs. 10. Active case detection methods, such as large-scale campaigns, are recommended in high-endemic areas or hard-to-reach regions. These efforts should focus on high-risk and vulnerable groups, including contacts of leprosy cases and children. 11. Retrospective screening of contacts of registered cases within the past five years can help detect leprosy early and prevent further transmission. 12. Diagnostic systems must ensure quality to avoid over-diagnosis and monitor the cost-effectiveness of active screening efforts. Laboratory services should be accessible for diagnostic confirmation when needed. 13. Integrated screening campaigns for leprosy and other diseases, such as tuberculosis or neglected tropical diseases, can be cost-effective and impactful. 14. Barriers to passive case finding, such as lack of awareness, fear of stigma, and physical or cultural challenges, must be addressed through public information campaigns, advocacy, and flexible service arrangements like mobile clinics. 15. In high-burden settings, active screening should target areas with higher-than-average detection rates, hard-to-reach regions, and specific groups like schoolchildren and contacts of leprosy cases. 16. Adequate human resources, including female staff and private examination areas, should be ensured for proper patient evaluation and classification. 17. Incentives for community healthcare workers can facilitate early suspicion and diagnosis of leprosy. Training programs should include leprosy in the curriculum for nurses, medical officers, and community health workers. 18. Expertise in pediatric leprosy detection and treatment should be available at referral centers, with specialized care models developed to prevent disabilities in children. 19. Awareness campaigns should be periodically repeated to sustain their impact and integrated with other health programs for cost-effectiveness. 20. National strategies, such as those implemented in India and Brazil, emphasize early detection, treatment, and public education to reduce stigma and improve leprosy control.
